Moving RRSP savings into an FHSA or keeping them for the Home Buyers’ Plan: FHSA room, the lost deduction and 15 years of repayments

A first-time buyer with RRSP savings has two ways to put them toward a home: transfer them into a First Home Savings Account, where a qualifying withdrawal is tax-free and nothing has to be paid back, or leave them in the RRSP and withdraw up to CAD 60,000 under the Home Buyers’ Plan, which has to be repaid over 15 years. A transfer is not deductible and uses FHSA room that new cash could have used for a deduction. This guide sets out the rules, compares three approaches over the years before a purchase, and shows when each one leaves more after tax, with CRA’s 2024 FHSA statistics and an editable scenario.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 10 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Over 3 years to a purchase at the end of 2028, contributions and transfers together can put at most $24,000 into the FHSA. Filling the room your cash leaves with an RRSP transfer moves $12,000 out of the RRSP. The best position after tax is “Cash first, RRSP transfer fills the rest of the room”: $50,478 of home cash and $46,326 after allowing 20% tax on RRSP money still to come out. Putting the transfer first instead gives up $3,600 of FHSA deduction refunds to move $12,000 more out of the RRSP. An HBP withdrawal of $20,760 in 2028 needs at least $1,384 a year from 2033 to 2047 under the extended relief. The RRSP holds only $20,760 by then, so the HBP is $4,240 short of the amount you entered. These are planning estimates with one return in every account, not CRA determinations.

The central idea

An RRSP-to-FHSA transfer (Form RC720) is not deductible, counts against the same CAD 8,000 a year and CAD 40,000 lifetime FHSA room as contributions, and does not give back RRSP deduction room. What it does is turn RRSP money, which is taxed when it comes out, into FHSA money that comes out tax-free for a qualifying home purchase and never has to be repaid. The Home Buyers’ Plan lends you up to CAD 60,000 of your own RRSP, but every dollar must go back over 15 years with after-tax cash; CRA’s overview page says that for a first withdrawal from 2026 to 2028 repayments start in the fifth year after. In the default example (CAD 30,000 in an RRSP, CAD 4,000 a year of new savings, a purchase at the end of 2028), putting the cash into the FHSA first and topping up the rest of the room from the RRSP gives the most home cash, CAD 50,478, and the best after-tax position. Moving the RRSP in first wins only when the tax rate on RRSP money in retirement is close to or above today’s rate.

01

Two routes from an RRSP to a down payment

Many first-time buyers already have an RRSP, often from a workplace plan or from contributions made to cut tax, before they open a First Home Savings Account. Since 2023 there have been two ways to put that money toward a home:

  • Transfer it into the FHSA. A direct transfer moves RRSP money into the FHSA without tax. When it comes out as a qualifying withdrawal for a first home, it is still tax-free, and nothing has to be paid back.
  • Leave it in the RRSP and use the Home Buyers’ Plan (HBP). Up to CAD 60,000 can be withdrawn without tax for a qualifying home, but it has to be repaid to an RRSP over 15 years. Repayments are not deductible.

The routes can be combined, and both can be used for the same home. The difficulty is that the FHSA has limited room. A dollar of room filled by an RRSP transfer is a dollar of room that new cash cannot use, and new cash put into an FHSA earns a deduction. The calculator compares three approaches over the years before the purchase: putting only new cash into the FHSA, putting cash in first and topping up the rest of the room from the RRSP, and moving the RRSP in first.

02

What CRA says about each route

RRSP-to-FHSA transferHome Buyers’ Plan withdrawal
HowDirect transfer with Form RC720, given to the financial institutionWithdrawal with Form T1036 under a written agreement to buy or build
LimitYour unused FHSA participation room at the time: CAD 8,000 a year plus up to CAD 8,000 carried forward, CAD 40,000 for life, shared with contributionsCAD 60,000 per participation period, from your own RRSPs
DeductionNone; the original RRSP contribution was already deductedNone on the withdrawal; repayments are not deductible
RRSP roomNot restoredNot used by repayments, which are designated on Schedule 7
Paying backNothing to repayFifteen yearly minimums, each the balance divided by the years left; a shortfall is added to income
When used for the homeQualifying FHSA withdrawal, tax-freeTax-free withdrawal, home bought or built before 1 October of the next year

On transfers, CRA’s transfers page says a direct RRSP transfer reduces unused FHSA participation room, must not exceed that room when it is made, is not deductible and does not restore unused RRSP deduction room. A transfer from a spousal RRSP is not allowed if the spouse or common-law partner contributed to a spousal RRSP in the same year or the two years before. On room, CRA’s participation room page counts contributions and RRSP transfers together against the same annual and lifetime limits. On the HBP, CRA’s overview gives the CAD 60,000 limit and says both routes can be used for the same home if the conditions are met at the time of each withdrawal.

03

When HBP repayments start: two CRA pages that disagree

Under the standard rule, HBP repayments start in the second year after the year of the first withdrawal. A temporary relief deferred the start to the fifth year after, for a first withdrawal from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2025. CRA’s HBP overview (page details 17 February 2026) says this relief has been extended to a first withdrawal from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2028, and gives the example that a first withdrawal in 2026 means a first repayment year of 2031. CRA’s repayment page (page details 20 January 2026) still describes only the 2022 to 2025 window.

The calculator follows the newer overview page by default and has a switch to use only the standard rule. Either way the size of each payment is the same: one-fifteenth of the withdrawal if every minimum is paid. What the relief changes is how long the money stays out of the RRSP before it has to go back. A repayment can be made in the year or in the first 60 days of the next year. Any part of a year’s minimum that is not repaid is added to income for that year, so it is taxed and is gone from the HBP balance for good.

04

Why the comparison turns on two tax rates

Treat each dollar by where it ends up.

  • Cash put into the FHSA earns a deduction at today’s marginal rate and comes out tax-free for the home.
  • Cash that cannot go into the FHSA because a transfer took the room goes into a TFSA or savings with no deduction. It is still tax-free, but the deduction is lost.
  • RRSP money transferred to the FHSA leaves the RRSP and becomes tax-free. Left in the RRSP, it would have been taxed at the retirement rate when it came out, so the transfer is worth the retirement rate on that money.
  • An HBP withdrawal gives tax-free cash now, but each dollar must be put back with after-tax cash, and that dollar is then taxed again at the retirement rate when it leaves the RRSP. Ignoring growth over the repayment years, it is a loan from yourself: it changes when you have the money, not how much you end with.

So with cash available, using room for a transfer instead of a contribution swaps a deduction at today’s rate for tax-free treatment at the retirement rate. When retirement income is expected to be lower, the cash should go into the FHSA first and the RRSP should fill only the room that cash cannot. When there is no new cash, a transfer is the only way to use the room, and it beats leaving the RRSP untouched at any positive retirement rate. The calculator counts RRSP money still in the plan at (1 − retirement rate) and each dollar still owed to the HBP at the retirement rate, so all three approaches are measured the same way at the purchase date.

05

Six worked cases

Each case starts with CAD 30,000 in an RRSP, opens a first FHSA in 2026 with CAD 8,000 of room, earns 4% a year in every account, and asks for a CAD 25,000 HBP withdrawal at the purchase. Today’s marginal rate is 30%. Figures are home cash at the purchase, then the after-tax position.

No new cashCAD 25,000 · 26,997CAD 33,746 · 32,191 (same as transfer first)CAD 33,746 · 32,191

In the default case the top-up approach moves CAD 12,000 from the RRSP over three years, leaving CAD 20,760 there by the end of 2028, so the HBP can only provide that much, not CAD 25,000. The minimum repayment is then CAD 1,384 a year from 2033 to 2047 under the extended relief. Moving the RRSP in first gives up CAD 3,600 of deduction refunds on CAD 12,000 of cash that went to a TFSA instead, and leaves only CAD 7,774 for the HBP. With CAD 8,000 a year of cash, the transfer-first approach shows more home cash but a weaker position, because it spends the deduction to empty an RRSP that would have been taxed at only 20%. At equal rates the transfer-first approach edges ahead by about CAD 150, because each year’s refund arrives a year late and transferred money starts growing tax-free earlier. In the five-year case the transfer-first approach empties the RRSP, so there is nothing left for the HBP, and the purchase in 2030 falls outside the relief window, so any HBP repayment would start in 2032. An independent Python check with 40-digit decimals reproduces every figure.

06

What CRA’s 2024 statistics show

CRA’s FHSA statistics for 2024 count 1.46 million holders with 1.68 million accounts. In that year 1.04 million holders contributed CAD 6.47 billion, an average of about CAD 6,231 each, and 146,400 holders, about 10% of all holders, withdrew CAD 1.76 billion, about CAD 12,034 each. The average withdrawal rose with the bracket, from about CAD 11,273 in the lowest to about CAD 14,051 in the highest, and 88.6% of all contributions came from holders in the two lowest brackets. CRA does not separate qualifying withdrawals for a home from taxable ones, and its contribution totals do not say how much arrived as RRSP transfers, so the statistics cannot show how often the transfer route is used. They do show that most FHSA money in 2024 came from people with taxable income below CAD 111,733, for whom the deduction on new cash is worth less and the case for a transfer depends more on the retirement rate.

07

Before you move anything

  1. Confirm your FHSA room. Room starts only when the first FHSA is opened, and all your FHSAs share it. Check My Account or your notice of assessment, and remember that a transfer above your room is an excess taxed at 1% a month.
  2. Use a direct transfer. Ask the institution for Form RC720. Withdrawing from the RRSP and depositing the cash yourself is an ordinary taxable RRSP withdrawal and a separate contribution.
  3. Put deductible cash first. If you have new savings, contribute them before filling the rest of the room with a transfer, unless you expect a retirement tax rate close to or above today’s.
  4. Leave room for the HBP if you need it. Moving the whole RRSP into the FHSA leaves nothing to withdraw under the HBP. Check that the two together still cover the down payment.
  5. Plan the repayments. If you use the HBP, put the first repayment year and the yearly minimum in your budget now. Repayments compete with new RRSP contributions, and a missed minimum becomes taxable income.
  6. Know the exit. If you do not buy a home, CRA’s FHSA overview says the savings can be transferred to an RRSP or RRIF without tax and without using RRSP room, so a transfer made in error is not lost.

08

What the calculator leaves out

  • Eligibility. It assumes you are a first-time home buyer for both the FHSA and the HBP, a Canadian resident, and that the purchase meets every condition at the time of each withdrawal.
  • Tax rates. Today’s and the retirement rates are single entered numbers. Provincial tax, benefits that depend on income and the option to carry the FHSA deduction forward are not calculated.
  • Returns. Every account earns the same fixed return. Markets can fall before the purchase.
  • TFSA room. Cash that does not go into the FHSA is assumed to fit in a TFSA.
  • Timing within a year. Deposits are at the start of each year, refunds arrive at the start of the next year and the purchase is at the end of the last year. The last refund is counted without growth, although it arrives after the purchase.
  • Growth during HBP repayments. The after-tax position values the HBP balance at the purchase date and ignores what the repaid money would earn later.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The first chart uses CRA’s First Home Savings Account Statistics for the 2024 tax year, Table 2 by federal tax bracket (page details 14 October 2026; data processed to 30 June 2026): holders, contributors, total contributions, holders who withdrew and total withdrawals, as CRA published them; the averages are calculations. The other five charts apply CRA’s pages on transfers into FHSAs (page details 17 August 2026), FHSA participation room (17 September 2026), the Home Buyers’ Plan (17 February 2026) and HBP repayments (20 January 2026), reviewed 27 October 2026, to an editable hypothetical saver who meets every eligibility condition. Every account earns the same return; deposits are made at the start of each year and the purchase is at the end of the last year. Provincial tax, the TFSA’s own limit, the timing of the deduction, market risk, closing costs and CRA’s assessment of eligibility are not modelled. These are planning estimates, not CRA’s determination. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
